question: For airframe ice to form in flight in cloud, the essential conditions are:

options.text: Supercooled liquid droplets, and an airframe at or below 0°C
A temperature inversion above the aircraft, with dry air below
Relative humidity above 50%, at any airframe temperature
Ice crystals in the cloud, and an airframe temperature above 0°C

explanation: Ice accretion in cloud or rain needs liquid water that freezes on impact, which needs a sub-zero airframe. Ice crystals alone simply bounce off.

question: A supercooled water droplet is:

options.text: A droplet that has frozen into a small transparent ice pellet
A droplet that is warmer than the air surrounding it
A droplet still liquid although its temperature is below 0°C
A droplet that contains a freezing nucleus and is about to freeze

explanation: Freezing nuclei are scarce, so droplets often remain liquid well below 0°C. They freeze when disturbed, for example by striking an aircraft.

question: Supercooled water droplets can exist in cloud at temperatures down to about:
explanation: Below about −40°C water freezes spontaneously, so only ice crystals (and at most very tiny droplets) remain.

question: Large supercooled droplets are typically found in:

options.text: Cirrus and cirrostratus at temperatures around −40°C
Clear air above the tropopause, at temperatures below −50°C
Stratus and stratocumulus at temperatures below about −20°C
Cumulus, cumulonimbus and nimbostratus, from 0°C to about −20°C

explanation: Strong updraughts and deep cloud allow droplets to grow large. Below about −20°C droplets are generally smaller because ice crystals grow at their expense.

question: As the temperature in a cloud falls below about −20°C, the supercooled droplets generally become:

options.text: Larger, because condensation onto them speeds up
Larger, because they collide with each other more often
Smaller and fewer, as ice crystals grow at their expense
Unchanged in size, but more numerous

explanation: The Bergeron process transfers water from droplets to ice crystals, so the remaining droplets become small. Icing risk decreases with temperature.

question: The aerodynamic effects of ice on the wing leading edges include:

options.text: More lift and less drag, because the leading edge is smoother
No change, unless the ice is more than about 10 cm thick
A lower stalling speed and less weight, because ice is light
Less lift, more drag, a higher stalling speed and more weight

explanation: Even a small roughness at the leading edge disrupts the airflow, reducing the maximum lift coefficient and increasing drag.

question: A layer of frost or ice with the roughness of coarse sandpaper on the upper wing can:

options.text: Have no effect at all, because the layer is so thin
Reduce lift by about 30% and increase drag by about 40%
Increase lift slightly by smoothing the boundary layer
Reduce lift by about 1% only, which can be ignored

explanation: Surface roughness at the front of the wing greatly degrades lift. That is why all frost must be removed before take-off.

question: Uneven ice on propeller blades is likely to cause:

options.text: Severe vibration, and airframe damage when pieces are thrown off
No noticeable effect on the engine or airframe
A reduction in engine temperature, but no other effect
An increase in propeller efficiency through extra blade area

explanation: Unequal shedding unbalances the propeller, and ice thrown off can strike the fuselage.

question: Ice blocking the pitot and static sources can cause errors in:

options.text: The fuel quantity indicators only
The magnetic compass and the clock only
The ASI, altimeter, VSI and Machmeter
The radio altimeter and the GPS only

explanation: All pressure instruments depend on the pitot-static system. That is why pitot and static heating is used.

question: In severe conditions, ice can accumulate at a rate of about:

options.text: About 1 inch (2.5 cm) per day
About 1 inch (2.5 cm) in 2 minutes
About 1 mm per hour
About 1 inch (2.5 cm) in each hour of flight

explanation: Severe icing can build up very quickly, which is why it requires immediate action to leave the conditions.

question: Clear (glaze) ice forms when:

options.text: Large droplets hit, part freezes at once, and the rest flows back before freezing
Water vapour sublimates directly onto a cold airframe in clear air
Small droplets freeze instantly where they hit, trapping air in between them
Wet snow sticks to the leading edges and is compacted by the airflow

explanation: Freezing releases latent heat, which slows the freezing of the rest of the droplet. The water spreads back over the surface and freezes into a dense, transparent layer.

question: For each degree below 0°C, the fraction of a supercooled droplet that freezes on impact is about:
explanation: The latent heat released by freezing warms the remaining water. At −10°C only about 10/80 of the droplet freezes immediately, so most flows back.

question: Clear ice is considered the most dangerous type of airframe ice because it:

options.text: Only forms on the windscreen, where it blocks the pilot's view
Builds up quickly, is dense and heavy, sticks hard and distorts the aerofoil
Forms only on the ground, and never in flight
Is light, brittle and easily removed by the pneumatic de-icing boots in flight

explanation: Its flowback and rapid accretion, combined with its weight and strong adhesion, make it hard to remove and damaging to aircraft performance.

question: Clear ice is most likely in:

options.text: Cumulus, cumulonimbus and nimbostratus, from 0°C to about −20°C
Clear air, at temperatures of about +5°C
Stratus and stratocumulus, at about −30°C
Cirrus and cirrostratus, at temperatures of about −50°C at high level

explanation: These clouds contain large droplets in high concentrations in that temperature range.

question: Rime ice forms when:

options.text: Rain falls from warmer air above into a sub-zero layer
Large droplets freeze slowly, with a great deal of flowback
Water vapour sublimates directly onto the airframe in clear air
Small droplets freeze almost instantly on impact, trapping air

explanation: Each tiny droplet freezes where it hits, leaving air between the particles. The result is white, opaque and brittle, growing forward from the leading edge.

question: Rime ice is:

options.text: Always more dangerous than clear ice, as it is heavier
Crystalline and feathery, formed only in clear air
White, opaque and light, with little or no flowback
Transparent, dense and heavy, with much flowback

explanation: Trapped air makes rime opaque. It is lighter and easier to remove than clear ice, but it can still distort the aerofoil and block intakes.

question: Rime ice is most likely in:

options.text: Only freezing rain, falling beneath a warm front
Layer clouds, and the colder parts of heap clouds
Only clear air, when a cold aircraft descends
Only cumulonimbus, at temperatures between 0 and −5°C

explanation: These clouds contain small supercooled droplets, which freeze on impact as rime.

question: Mixed ice occurs when:

options.text: Hoar frost and rime form together in clear air below cloud
Rain and snow fall together at temperatures of about +5°C near the ground
The aircraft flies above the freezing level in completely dry air
Both large and small supercooled droplets are present, usually 0°C to −20°C

explanation: The small droplets form rime and the large droplets give clear ice with flowback, combining the worst features of both.

question: Rain ice (freezing rain) occurs when:

options.text: Cloud droplets freeze inside a cumulonimbus at about −30°C
Hail falls below the freezing level and melts into large drops
Rain from a warm layer aloft falls into sub-zero air, supercools and freezes on impact
Snow falls through a warm layer near the ground and melts into cold rain drops before landing

explanation: The rain forms in air above 0°C, falls into a sub-zero layer near the ground and becomes supercooled. Large drops strike the aircraft and freeze with much flowback.

question: Rain ice is typically found:

options.text: In a shallow layer at low level ahead of a warm front or occlusion in winter
Behind a cold front in summer, in the cumulonimbus showers of polar air
In the anvil of a cumulonimbus, at about −40°C
At the tropopause near jet streams, in thin cirrus

explanation: Warm air overrunning cold air at a warm front provides the warm layer aloft and the freezing layer below.

question: An aircraft meets heavy rain ice ahead of a warm front. The most appropriate immediate action is usually to:

options.text: Leave the conditions at once, for example by turning back or climbing into the warm layer
Turn off all the ice protection systems to save bleed air for the engines
Reduce speed and continue straight ahead until the rain stops of its own accord
Descend further into the colder layer below, where the rain will be frozen solid already

explanation: Rain ice builds up extremely rapidly. The usual advice is to turn back at once; climbing into the warm layer above is also an option if it is near and the aircraft can do so.

question: Rain ice is particularly common in winter over:

options.text: The Sahara and North Africa
North America and central Europe
The equatorial Pacific islands
The Arabian Peninsula

explanation: Strong continental cold at the surface with warm air overrunning it provides frequent freezing rain events.

question: Pack snow on an aircraft is caused by:

options.text: Hail bouncing off the wings and collecting
Ice crystals alone, sublimating onto the cold skin of the aircraft
Snow mixed with supercooled droplets; it can block intakes
Rain falling into air that is above freezing

explanation: Supercooled water binds the snow together so that it packs into openings and intakes. Its effects are usually slight.

question: Hoar frost is:

options.text: Rime ice formed from small supercooled droplets in stratus
Frozen rain from a warm front, falling into a cold layer
Clear ice formed from large supercooled droplets inside a cumulonimbus
A white crystalline deposit formed by vapour depositing on a sub-zero surface

explanation: Hoar frost forms without passing through the liquid phase, much like frost on a car on a clear cold night.

question: Hoar frost may form in flight when:

options.text: An aircraft flies through the core of a large cumulonimbus with heavy rain
A cold-soaked aircraft descends quickly into, or climbs into, warmer moist air
An aircraft flies in heavy rain at temperatures above 0°C
An aircraft flies through very dry air at high level

explanation: The cold skin brings the adjacent moist air to its frost point, and vapour sublimates onto it.

question: Hoar frost on the ground must be removed before take-off mainly because:

options.text: It turns into clear ice at take-off speed, blocking the pitot tubes
It increases the lift, which makes the take-off speeds unreliable
It is very heavy, so the aircraft may exceed its maximum take-off mass
It adds skin friction and drag, can reduce lift, and obscures windscreens

explanation: Even a thin deposit roughens the surfaces enough to lengthen the take-off run and degrade lift.

question: In-flight hoar frost is normally:

options.text: Not severe, and cleared by flying into warmer air or by kinetic heating
Impossible to remove until the aircraft has landed
The most dangerous of all forms of icing
Severe, so that immediate diversion is necessary to keep the aircraft safe

explanation: The deposit is thin and light. It disappears as the airframe warms.

question: Icing in cloud is usually most severe in:

options.text: Altostratus and altocumulus
Cirrostratus and cirrus
Cumulus and cumulonimbus
Thin stratus and stratocumulus

explanation: Strong updraughts in heap clouds support high concentrations of large supercooled droplets. Nimbostratus is moderate to severe; most other layer clouds are light.

question: Within a cumulus cloud, the concentration of supercooled water is usually greatest:

options.text: Below the cloud base, in the falling rain
In the anvil, where the cloud spreads out
In the lower part of the cloud, just above the freezing level
At the very top of the cloud, where it is coldest and the updraught strongest

explanation: The warmer air near the base condensed the most water. Higher in the cloud more water has been converted to ice or fallen out.

question: A cloud with a high base temperature will tend to give:

options.text: Only hoar frost, because the cloud is warm
More severe icing above the freezing level, from more liquid water
Less severe icing, because clouds with warm bases are always thin
No icing at all, because the cloud base is above 0°C

explanation: Warmer air holds more water vapour, so more water condenses as it rises. The water content at any sub-zero level is higher.

question: Which aircraft components collect ice most rapidly?

options.text: The flat sides of the fuselage
Thick, broad wing roots close to the fuselage, where the airflow slows
The trailing edges at the rear of the wings
Thin parts such as tailplane edges, struts, aerials and probes

explanation: Thin bodies deflect the airflow less, so more droplets strike them. A little ice on the main wing may mean more on thinner parts.

question: Higher airspeed increases the rate of ice accretion because:

options.text: The aircraft meets more droplets each second, though kinetic heating may offset this
Higher speed always lowers the skin temperature through adiabatic cooling of the air
Higher speed makes the droplets larger as they approach the aircraft
Higher speed stops all kinetic heating of the airframe

explanation: Catch rate rises with speed. At high speed kinetic heating may raise the skin above 0°C and prevent ice.

question: Kinetic heating of the airframe can be estimated as (TAS/100)² °C. At a TAS of 300 kt this is about:
explanation: (300/100)² = 9°C. The skin may therefore be warmer than the outside air.

question: Kinetic heating that raises the skin temperature but leaves it still below 0°C may:

options.text: Increase the risk, by making more of each droplet flow back before freezing
Remove all icing, because the skin is now warmer than the outside air
Have no effect at all on the ice that forms
Turn rime ice into hoar frost on the leading edges

explanation: A skin just below 0°C freezes droplets slowly, giving clear ice. Only if the skin rises above 0°C does kinetic heating protect it.

question: Below about −40°C, the icing risk in cloud is usually:

options.text: Severe, because the droplets are largest at that temperature
The same as at −5°C, because temperature does not matter
Moderate clear ice, because of the high water content
Negligible, as only very tiny droplets, if any, remain

explanation: At very low temperatures the cloud is almost entirely ice crystals, which do not adhere.

question: Moderate icing is defined in reports as icing where:

options.text: There is no accumulation at all
Even short encounters become potentially hazardous, so ice protection or diversion is necessary
Ice is just perceptible and not hazardous
Ice protection fails to control the accumulation at all, so immediate diversion is needed

explanation: Moderate icing calls for use of ice protection or a change of heading or altitude. Severe icing calls for immediate diversion because the equipment cannot cope.

question: Severe icing is defined in reports as icing where:

options.text: Ice is just perceptible, with accretion only slightly faster than sublimation, for over an hour
Occasional use of the ice protection equipment removes or prevents the ice
Ice protection cannot reduce or control the build-up, so immediate diversion is needed
Ice forms only on the windscreen and does not affect handling

explanation: The ICAO description is conditions in which an immediate change of heading and/or altitude is considered essential.

question: Light icing is icing in which:

options.text: Ice might become a problem after about an hour, but occasional use of protection removes it
Ice builds up so fast that the protection equipment cannot keep up with the accretion
No ice forms at all, even without any ice protection
Immediate diversion is necessary because the hazard cannot be controlled

explanation: Light icing is manageable with intermittent use of de-icing or anti-icing systems.

question: Airframe icing is forecast mainly by forecasting:

options.text: The height of the tropopause along the route
The surface pressure tendency over three hours
The surface wind speed and direction forecast at the destination aerodrome
The type and vertical extent of cloud and the temperatures within it

explanation: Icing depends on cloud type, droplet size and temperature, so the forecast is built from cloud and freezing level forecasts.

question: The freezing level is:

options.text: The height at which supercooled droplets freeze spontaneously
The height at which the air temperature is 0°C
The height of the cloud base
The height of the tropopause

explanation: It is shown in forecasts as the height of the 0°C isotherm. Where there is an inversion, there may be more than one freezing level.

question: In southern England the average freezing level is about:

options.text: 1000 ft all year
3000 ft in February and 11 000 ft in August
11 000 ft in February and 3000 ft in August
20 000 ft all year

explanation: The freezing level follows the seasonal temperature cycle, lowest in late winter and highest in late summer.

question: With a temperature inversion above sub-zero air near the ground, it is possible to have:

options.text: No freezing level at all
A freezing level below the ground
A freezing level exactly at the tropopause
Two or more freezing levels

explanation: Temperature passes through 0°C at the bottom of the warm layer and again above it, so there are multiple 0°C levels. This is the setting for freezing rain.

question: Carburettor icing is caused by:

options.text: Cooling from fuel evaporation and from expansion in the venturi
High oil temperatures that cause the fuel to vaporise
Hoar frost forming on the cylinder heads in clear air
Supercooled droplets striking the propeller and being ingested

explanation: Fuel evaporation absorbs latent heat and the venturi lowers the pressure and temperature of the air, so ice can form even when outside air is well above 0°C.

question: Carburettor icing can occur at outside air temperatures:

options.text: Only below about −20°C, in very cold and dry winter air
Only above about +30°C, in very humid air
Well above 0°C, roughly −10°C to +25°C or more in moist air
Only below 0°C, in visible moisture

explanation: The internal cooling can be 20°C or more, so carburettor ice is possible on warm, humid days, especially at low power.

question: For a fuel-injected or turbocharged piston engine, the main induction icing hazard is:

options.text: Ice forming in the carburettor venturi from fuel evaporation
Impact ice on the air intake from snow or supercooled water
Fuel boiling in the injection lines at altitude
Hoar frost forming inside the cylinders on descent

explanation: Without a carburettor there is no venturi or fuel-evaporation cooling, but intakes and filters can still ice over.

question: In a turbine engine, icing can occur in the intake even when the outside air is slightly above 0°C because:

options.text: Fuel evaporating in the intake absorbs latent heat and chills the air
The compressor blades are always below 0°C, whatever the outside air temperature may be
Air accelerating into the intake cools adiabatically, especially at high RPM and low speed
Hoar frost forms on the turbine blades from the exhaust gases

explanation: Intake suction lowers the pressure and temperature by several degrees, so engine anti-ice is normally required in visible moisture below about +10°C.

question: Ice can form on the upper wing surface of a parked aircraft in rain or drizzle with an air temperature above 0°C because:

options.text: The rain is always supercooled
Kinetic heating stops on the ground
The air above the wing is colder than the surroundings
Very cold fuel in the wing tanks keeps the skin below 0°C

explanation: After a long flight at high altitude, cold-soaked fuel chills the wing skin. Clear ice can form and may be hidden under snow; ice shedding at take-off is dangerous to rear-mounted engines.

question: Using anti-icing or de-icing equipment normally:

options.text: Carries a penalty, such as bleed-air use or extra drag
Reduces the fuel consumption
Has no effect on performance at all
Increases the available engine thrust slightly at all settings

explanation: Bleed air and electrical power for ice protection reduce available thrust and increase fuel burn.

question: Supercooled large droplets (SLD) such as freezing drizzle and freezing rain are dangerous because:

options.text: They can strike and freeze aft of the area protected by ice protection
They occur only at very high levels, above about FL300
They cannot form ice at all because they are too large
They only form a thin layer of rime on the very leading edge of the wing

explanation: Large drops have more inertia, impinge further aft on the wing and spread before freezing, forming ridges of ice beyond the boots or heated area.

question: An aircraft flying in stratocumulus at −6°C is most likely to accumulate:

options.text: Hoar frost only
No ice, because stratocumulus contains only ice crystals
Severe clear ice at a very high rate
Rime or mixed ice of light to moderate intensity

explanation: Layer cloud contains relatively small supercooled droplets, so the typical accretion is rime of light to moderate intensity.

question: An aircraft in nimbostratus at −3°C, with large droplets, is likely to accumulate:

options.text: Only hoar frost
Only rime from small droplets
Clear ice, possibly moderate to severe
No ice, as the temperature is too warm

explanation: Near 0°C large droplets freeze slowly, flowing back to form clear ice. Nimbostratus can give a large accumulation.

question: Which combination gives the greatest icing risk?

options.text: Ice crystals in high concentration at about −50°C
Large supercooled droplets in high concentration just below 0°C
Dry air with no cloud at about −10°C
Small droplets in low concentration at about −35°C in thin cloud

explanation: Large drops and high water content near 0°C give rapid build-up of clear ice.

question: Ice protection systems are of two types:

options.text: Anti-icing, which prevents ice, and de-icing, which removes it once formed
Pressurised systems and unpressurised systems for each surface
Mechanical systems and chemical systems, never electrical ones
Heating systems and cooling systems, both of which are run from engine bleed air

explanation: Heated leading edges are typically anti-icing; pneumatic boots are de-icing systems that need some ice to break off.

question: Before take-off in frost conditions, wings must be:

options.text: Covered with a thin layer of water to melt any frost that forms
Cleared only on the upper surface near the wingtips, where the ailerons are
Left as they are if the frost is thin, as it blows off in the take-off run
Free of frost, ice and snow, as even a thin layer can seriously reduce lift

explanation: The "clean wing" concept: contamination must be removed and, where necessary, anti-icing fluid applied.

question: Hold-over time for de-icing fluid is:

options.text: The time taken for the fluid to dry completely on the surfaces
The maximum flight time allowed after the aircraft has been de-iced
The estimated time the fluid will keep ice and snow from forming or sticking
The time it takes the ground crew to apply the fluid to the whole aircraft

explanation: Hold-over time depends on fluid type, concentration, temperature and the type and intensity of precipitation.

question: An increase in airspeed of a jet in cloud near −3°C may:

options.text: Cause hoar frost to form on the leading edges
Raise the skin above 0°C by kinetic heating, reducing accretion
Have no effect on the skin temperature at all
Always increase ice accretion, whatever the outside temperature

explanation: Kinetic heating of several degrees can lift the skin above freezing, while a smaller rise may only slow freezing and produce clear ice.
